title: Georgetown Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Georgetown wells have a 70-foot median depth, with fractured-bedrock conditions and finished-well costs of $10,600-$19,000.
h1: Georgetown, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Georgetown means looking closely at the well record, not just the listing description. Within five miles of town, Colorado DWR records include 652 permitted wells, but only 329 are recorded as constructed. Depth and yield information is also incomplete: 308 wells report total depth, 86 report pump yield, and 24 report static water level.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That fits the mountain setting around Georgetown, Silver Plume, and Empire, where granite and gneiss can make nearby wells perform differently. Use this page to set expectations, then verify the specific parcel, permit, well construction, water rights, septic layout, and access before you buy.

sections.heading: Georgetown well depths depend on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Georgetown is 70 feet. The middle half runs from 38 to 121 feet, so a driller’s bid near the median may be reasonable for a favorable site, but it should not be treated as a guarantee. Sixty-six percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 24% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 6% are 300 to 600 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well is 1,201 feet. The spread reflects fractured granite and gneiss rather than a uniform shallow aquifer. A neighboring well in Silver Plume or Empire can provide useful context, but it does not remove the need for a site-specific estimate. Ask what depth range the bid covers and what happens if the first fracture zones do not produce.

sections.heading: Most Georgetown wells report useful household-scale yields
sections.html:
Among the 86 wells with pump-yield records, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 7.4 to 12.8 gallons per minute. Eighty percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 15% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No recorded well in this dataset is under 1 gallon per minute, while 5% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is a generally workable production range for a household, but a yield test is still important. A pump rating is not the same as dependable storage in the well or a guarantee during drought. Confirm the permitted use, tested yield, pressure tank arrangement, and any storage system. Most permits are for domestic or household use, at 70% of the listed use mix.

sections.heading: The water table is often reachable, but the trend is not proven
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 34 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 65 feet. In practical terms, many recorded wells had water standing relatively close to the surface when measured, even though the completed well may be deeper. Static level is not the same as pumping level, and it can change with season, recharge, and nearby use.

The records contain static water-level information for only 24 wells. They do not provide enough reported measurements here to establish a reliable long-term decline or rise in the water table. Ask for the well’s static and pumping levels, the measurement date, and a recent production test. A driller should also explain how the pump will be set below the expected pumping level without overestimating available storage.

sections.heading: Permit history shows steady development around Georgetown
sections.html:
Permit activity began in the records in the 1950s, with one permit issued in that decade. Activity increased through the following decades: 9 in the 1960s, 65 in the 1970s, 71 in the 1980s, 97 in the 1990s, 191 in the 2000s, 61 in the 2010s, and 32 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 33 wells; Mcpherson Drilling Company (Mcpherson, Benny Don), with 29; and James Drilling (Keaton, Jordan K.), with 23. These names describe recorded permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Before closing, pull the DWR permit and construction records for the property and ask who completed the well, when it was tested, and whether the permit matches the intended household use.

sections.heading: A Georgetown well budget starts with the rock
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock around Georgetown, the drilling rate model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the recorded median depth of 70 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $4,600 to $7,000. That is only the drilling portion. A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $10,600 to $19,000.

Deeper-than-expected drilling is the main reason a bid can move beyond the initial allowance. Access, casing and grout requirements, difficult ground, electrical distance, trenching, and pump equipment can also change the final invoice. Have the contractor separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump installation, storage, trenching, and electrical work. A low per-foot number is not a complete project price.

sections.heading: Mines, water quality, and site layout deserve a close check
sections.html:
The area within about 10 miles contains 2,136 historic mine features, 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. Those mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test rather than assume the water is safe. Request a complete potable-water panel appropriate to the parcel’s history, and ask for any prior laboratory reports.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured rock even when nearby wells are productive. Check casing, grout, wellhead protection, and the distance between the well and proposed septic components. The property also needs a workable access route for drilling equipment, a building location that protects the well, and enough room for septic installation and replacement areas. Confirm DWR requirements and any water-rights or augmentation issue before construction.

sections.heading: What to verify before buying or building near Georgetown
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s own permit, well construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and recorded use. Then compare nearby wells in Georgetown, Silver Plume, Empire, and Idaho Springs for depth, yield, static level, and aquifer description. Neighboring records help frame the geology, but the property’s fracture zones control the result.

For a vacant lot, get a driller’s access review and a written budget that includes the complete well system, not just the hole. Confirm that the proposed house, driveway, septic system, and well can fit together on the site. For an existing home, have the well and pressure system inspected, test the water, and verify that the permit and actual use agree. Colorado’s 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit does not remove the need to understand the permit’s specific conditions.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Georgetown, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 70 feet, and the middle half of reported wells is 38 to 121 feet. Sixty-six percent are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 1,201 feet. Georgetown’s fractured granite and gneiss make depth highly site-specific, so nearby well records are useful for planning but cannot guarantee your lot’s result.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Georgetown?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, drilling is estimated at $4,600 to $7,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,600 to $19,000. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, grout, and electrical distance can change the final price.

faq.q: How much water does a Georgetown well produce?
faq.a: Among 86 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 7.4 to 12.8 gallons per minute. Eighty percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe recorded tests, not a promise for a new well. Request a current yield test and review the well’s pumping level and storage.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Georgetown, Colorado?
faq.a: The records identify 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 2,136 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Those locations do not establish contamination at your well. Test the water through a qualified laboratory, review prior results, and consider the parcel’s mining history, septic layout, casing, and wellhead protection before using it for drinking.

faq.q: Are Georgetown wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a long-term water-table trend because only 24 wells report static water levels. Those reports have a median depth to water of 34 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 65 feet. A production test, current static and pumping levels, and neighboring well records are more useful for judging a specific property than the area median alone.
